title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating under shared_initial_candidate semantics. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). No automated repairs were applied. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null outcome, and concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs to avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are being proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows. Safe operational adoption requires demonstrating that model outputs will not introduce reachability, policy, or sequencing violations when applied to networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures combining generation with external deterministic verification and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited.

Research question. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial sampled candidate reused by both arms per intent), does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to that identical sampled candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing the same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and executed a fully preregistered confirmatory run (autocand_A1_prereg_v1).

Contributions. (i) A preregistered paired design and frozen execution with shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; (ii) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents; (iii) artifact‑grounded results showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and zero repair activity; (iv) an interpretation grounded in archived artifacts explaining the degenerate null and its contributors; and (v) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑ups that avoid ceiling effects.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps research covers intent→config translation, runbook generation, RCA, and early agentic automation proposals. Recent surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1],[2],[4]. In adjacent domains, generate→validate→repair architectures have been proposed and demonstrated in domain‑specific studies: program repair and DevOps prototypes (RepairAgent) and verification modeling (VeriFlow) provide concrete examples where external verification or repair logic is combined with generation to reduce observed failures under specific datasets and validators [5],[6]. These prior works motivate validator‑coupled evaluations but do not remove the need for experimental designs that isolate validator effects from model sampling variance.

Methodological gap addressed. Two gaps motivated our paired design. First, pipeline comparisons that permit different first‑pass draws per arm confound validator effects with model sampling variance. Second, many benchmarks emphasize QA/relevance metrics or log/RCA tasks but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. Our shared_initial_candidate experiment isolates the validator/gate effect on identical initial generations and therefore directly addresses the first gap.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design freeze. We preregistered the study as autocand_A1_prereg_v1. The plan fixed: primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate; model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1); deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy; repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents); and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). These parameters were archived prior to execution and are recorded in the execution manifest.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and inferential meaning. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the experiment produces exactly one initial generation per intent that is deterministically reused by both arms. Consequently the confirmatory estimand measures only the validator/repair/gate effect on that same first‑pass candidate; it does not measure effects due to guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, multiple independent samples, or model variance.

Models, adapter, validator, and configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and provider = "openai_responses"). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style checks (sequence ordering, interface precondition checks, final_group and minimum_up constraints, protected interfaces, and reachability/policy consistency). The recorded model configuration includes max_output_tokens = 2000, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, reasoning_effort = "minimal", and temperature = null. Important clarification (recorded here per reviewer request): temperature = null as recorded in the model configuration is not evidence that model sampling was deterministic (it does not imply temperature = 0), and the adapter does not guarantee deterministic sampling. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics control the paired comparison by reusing a single sampled generation per pair; we do not claim deterministic model sampling.

Task bank, deterministic sampling, and constraints. The deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced intent→configuration items with embedded constraints (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, workflow_policies, and explicit required_sequence). The preregistered sampler selected 200 paired intents using the adapter's deterministic index rule; selection was fixed and outcome‑independent. Per‑task difficulty metadata (labels such as "very_hard" and "extreme") are encoded in the archived task manifest; the manifest indicates the suite is dominated by items labeled "very_hard" with a minority labeled "extreme" (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).

Interventions and primary outcome. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate (no gating). Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the deterministic gate applied a preregistered accept/reject rule and, upon violations, allowed up to one automated repair attempt. Primary binary outcome: unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization. Scoring used the rule full_intent_constraint_validation and returned codes such as VALID_CONFIGURATION or explicit violation codes. Per‑episode validator traces, repair flags, and scores were archived.

Confirmatory analysis (frozen). The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 on the 2×2 paired contingency of unsafe_flag across the 200 pairs. The executor reports discordant counts n10 (guarded_only) and n01 (baseline_only), an exact two‑sided test (McNemar equivalent), and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and preregistered retry rules for infrastructure failures were enforced. All run artifacts and analysis logs were preserved.

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). The paired contingency table is: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Therefore every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. The exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). Repair activity and diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; repair_provider_trace_path fields are null in the scoring artifacts. Observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, and required_command_count for representative tasks are recorded in the per‑episode validator traces.

Deterministic reconciliation confirms pair accounting and audit consistency (episode_accounting_consistent = true).

Latency notes. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics required one model call per pair, model_call accounting equals 200. The guarded pipeline executed validator checks but applied no repairs; timing logs show validator execution added measurable wall time per pair and the archived logs contain full timing distributions for reproducibility.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; consequently the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The archived artifacts (paired contingency, per‑episode validator traces, and model/provider audit) directly support this interpretation.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. Because there are no discordant pairs, every bootstrap resample of the paired outcomes yields the same paired difference (0.0), producing zero empirical variance and a degenerate CI [0.0,0.0]. This behavior is a legitimate inferential outcome and is recorded in the analysis log (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000).

Ceiling‑effect contributors (artifact‑traceable). The artifacts indicate three concrete contributors: (1) task‑bank alignment — the task generator produced required_sequence lists and workflow_policies closely matching the prompt schema, increasing the probability of syntactically correct mappings; (2) validator alignment — the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule set encoded sequencing and precondition checks aligned to the generator's required_sequence constraints, enabling correct syntactic candidates to pass validation readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics — by design the guarded arm could not trigger alternative first‑pass generations that might have been rejected and repaired. Each contributor is traceable in the archived task_manifest entries and per‑episode validator traces.

Design recommendations supported by artifacts. To measure verifier/gate value under nondegenerate conditions we recommend (artifact‑supported): (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates (the generator supports deterministic seeds and adjustable payloads); (b) switching to an independent‑generation per‑condition confirmatory design or sampling multiple generations per condition (this requires additional model calls and changes the estimand to capture guarded‑conditioned regeneration/model variance); (c) testing multiple model variants or nondefault sampling settings to reveal model variance effects (execution/model_configuration.json records requested_model and temperature fields and can be adapted); (d) increasing the automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness when violations are nontrivial; and (e) including human‑in‑the‑loop arms to assess operator responses to validator flags.

Operational caveats. The null result does not imply deterministic validators are without value in more realistic or adversarial regimes; rather it demonstrates that design choices (task bank, generation semantics, validator rules) determine whether a paired shared‑candidate contrast can detect verifier value. For operational claims, field trials, adversarial injections, and HITL evaluations are necessary.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic task bank, deterministic sampling rule, validator ruleset, and shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes. We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally raise baseline unsafe rates, allow independent per‑condition generation, or increase repair budgets to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or sampling variance.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions or vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the preregistered power targeted ~10 percentage‑point reductions but does not rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time or deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest encodes per‑task difficulty labels; the manifest indicates the suite is dominated by items labeled 'very_hard' with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
